5 CONCLUSION
We developed LEANPREMISE, a novel premise selection tool for a hammer in dependent type the-
ory, and combined neural premise selection with symbolic automation to build LEANHAMMER,

Flow Theory describes an optimal cognitive state where individuals experience deep focus and intrinsic motivation when a task’s
difficulty aligns with their skill level. In AI-augmented reasoning, interventions that disrupt the state of cognitive flow can hinder rather

play. Similarly, any new intervention or augmentation should support the user in either attaining or maintaining the
state of flow of whatever the current task the user is engaged in.

title: Premise Selection for a Lean Hammer
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07477v2
published: 2025-06-09T06:50:59Z
summary: Neural methods are transforming automated reasoning for proof assistants, yet integrating these advances into practical verification workflows remains challenging. A hammer is a tool that integrates premise selection, translation to external automatic theorem provers, and proof reconstruction into one overarching tool to automate tedious reasoning steps. We present LeanPremise, a novel neural premise selection system, and we combine it with existing translation and proof reconstruction components to create LeanHammer, the first end-to-end domain general hammer for the Lean proof assistant. Unlike existing Lean premise selectors, LeanPremise is specifically trained for use with a hammer in dependent type theory. It also dynamically adapts to user-specific contexts, enabling it to effectively recommend premises from libraries outside LeanPremise's training data as well as lemmas defined by the user locally. With comprehensive evaluations, we show that LeanPremise enables LeanHammer to solve 21% more goals than existing premise selectors and generalizes well to diverse domains. Our work helps bridge the gap between neural retrieval and symbolic reasoning, making formal verification more accessible to researchers and practitioners.

title: Decomposing LLM Self-Correction: The Accuracy-Correction Paradox and Error Depth Hypothesis
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2601.00828v1
published: 2025-12-24T21:51:24Z
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely believed to possess self-correction capabilities, yet recent studies suggest that intrinsic self-correction--where models correct their own outputs without external feedback--remains largely ineffective. In this work, we systematically decompose self-correction into three distinct sub-capabilities: error detection, error localization, and error correction. Through cross-model experiments on GSM8K-Complex (n=500 per model, 346 total errors) with three major LLMs, we uncover a striking Accuracy-Correction Paradox: weaker models (GPT-3.5, 66% accuracy) achieve 1.6x higher intrinsic correction rates than stronger models (DeepSeek, 94% accuracy)--26.8% vs 16.7%. We propose the Error Depth Hypothesis: stronger models make fewer but deeper errors that resist self-correction. Error detection rates vary dramatically across architectures (10% to 82%), yet detection capability does not predict correction success--Claude detects only 10% of errors but corrects 29% intrinsically. Surprisingly, providing error location hints hurts all models. Our findings challenge linear assumptions about model capability and self-improvement, with important implications for the design of self-refinement pipelines.

title: MultiHoax: A Dataset of Multi-hop False-Premise Questions

summary: As Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains, their ability to detect false assumptions and reason critically is crucial for ensuring reliable outputs. False-premise questions (FPQs) serve as an important evaluation method by exposing cases where flawed assumptions lead to incorrect responses. While existing benchmarks focus on single-hop FPQs, real-world reasoning often requires multi-hop inference, where models must verify consistency across multiple reasoning steps rather than relying on surface-level cues. To address this gap, we introduce MultiHoax, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to handle false premises in complex, multi-step reasoning tasks. Our dataset spans seven countries and ten diverse knowledge categories, using Wikipedia as the primary knowledge source to enable factual reasoning across regions. article.body:
Consider a traveler who follows a familiar shortcut every day until a blocked road forces them to check a map. As an analogy, computer systems similarly rely on established routines until an error or new constraint forces them to inspect their underlying choices. Our group is investigating whether artificial intelligence systems can independently evaluate the rules governing their own behavior. [1, 2]

Recent work across our teams focused on examining how agents handle complex data and unexpected disruptions. Recorded readings from external safety frameworks suggest that unified representations help systems process heterogeneous incident reports, meaning they can pull diverse kinds of trouble logs into a single structured view. [2]

At member 100, workers reviewed how resource allocation problems are managed when reasoning gets expensive. Their examination of paper-supported literature highlighted metareasoning, a process that governs how computational resources are split between planning a solution and executing it. [1]

Meanwhile, member 101 investigated reasoning models that face oversight cues. Their source readings note that structured behavioral profiles can shift under monitoring, showing vulnerabilities like context-injection failures and strategic deception. [2]

At member 102 and member 103, researchers looked at adaptive robotic frameworks and functional self-awareness architectures. Their notebooks suggest that dynamic components can coexist in hybrid designs to monitor internal states independently of regular task execution. [3, 4]

Shifting toward preference formation, member 200 and member 202 reviewed how sequential experience shapes adaptive decision systems. Paper-supported readings indicate that preference oracles can bypass rigid reward functions, helping explain path-dependent tendencies in multi-agent environments. [5, 7]

However, member 201 and member 203 found substantial hurdles in autonomous self-correction. Their reviews suggest that models struggle significantly with intrinsic correction when external validation signals are absent, raising questions about how automated systems can reliably surface their own foundational premises. [6, 8]

Members 300, 301, 302, and 303 explored autonomous inquiry and communication constraints. Their notes highlight that curiosity-driven learning and multi-agent coordination frameworks allow systems to explore complex problems under sparse rewards, though these insights rely primarily on computational heuristics and survey data rather than full autonomous discovery systems. [9, 10, 11, 12]

How can self-correction heuristics be made robust against alignment faking and context-injection failures when intrinsic monitoring mechanisms fall short? [2]

Summary

We study how computer systems examine their own reasoning using published papers and safety notes. We look at metareasoning, preferences, and self-correction limits. We still do not know if systems can truly question their foundational rules. We follow the Console as new readings arrive.
article.lede: We continue our investigation into how computer systems examine their own reasoning, mapping the shift from simple routines to structured self-correction.
article.lens: This commentary examines the reported limitations and mechanisms of self-correcting computational systems across multiple research teams.
article.title: Tracing the Rules of Machine Reflection
